summary:
NextCrop is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform. Farmers select their region, planting month, and irrigation status (irrigated or rain-fed). The platform then recommends a crop rotation cycle organized by plant families (legumes, cereals, nightshades, etc.), suggesting five crops.It displays the risk level (salinity, soil moisture, evapotranspiration) and the estimated financial return (the total price for which the farmer can potentially sell his harvest).

It addresses the challenge of farming under uncertainty: many farmers choose crops out of habit, without data, leading to losses, soil depletion, and unstable income. NextCrop replaces guesswork with personalized, location- and season-based recommendations, while promoting crop rotation to preserve soil fertility.

It matters because it helps farmers increase income, reduce risk, and farm more sustainably, especially in the face of water scarcity and climate change.
details:
What it does and how it works

NextCrop is a website that helps Moroccan farmers decide which crops to plant and when. The farmer draws the field as a polygon on a Mapbox map, says whether it is irrigated or rain-fed, picks a sowing month, and enters the last crop harvested.

The system then does the following.

  1. It places the field in one of the six agro-ecological zones of the FAO crop calendar.
  2. It picks the next crop family in a five-stage rotation. The order is legumes, poaceae, brassicas, umbellifers and alliums, then nightshades and cucurbits.
  3. It keeps only the crops the FAO crop calendar allows to be sown in that zone and month.
  4. It reads the field’s conditions, averaged over the polygon. Temperature, sunlight and rainfall come from NASA POWER. Soil pH, texture, organic carbon and nitrogen come from SoilGrids. Altitude comes from SRTM, and soil salinity from the FAO salinity raster.
  5. It scores each candidate crop from 0 to 100 by comparing those conditions with the crop’s requirements in FAO ECOCROP. One very unfavourable factor lowers the score sharply.
  6. It builds a timeline in which each crop is sown when the previous one is harvested. The result is a full rotation with sowing and harvest dates, the best alternatives for each stage, and an income estimate in MAD based on FAOSTAT yields and producer prices.

The site also reports four kinds of field risk.

  • Soil salinity: It gives a salinity level, lowers the scores of salt-sensitive crops, and recommends a conductivity test when salinity is high.
  • Water availability: It compares rainfall with the multi-year average and with crop needs. If rainfall is too low for rain-fed farming, it suggests irrigation.
  • Vegetation health: It analyses up to two years of NASA MODIS NDVI satellite images around the field and compares them with the previous year and with rainfall. It then gives a low, moderate or high risk level in plain language.
  • Warnings: It flags weak matches, waiting periods between crops and missing data.

It also lists the crops it ruled out, with a reason for each, such as “cannot be sown in this month in this zone” or “scores 25/100, held back by salinity”.

Benefits

  • Farmers get a complete rotation plan with dates, not a single crop suggestion.
  • It uses free, open data, so a first recommendation needs no laboratory analysis.
  • Every recommendation comes with a score, a limiting factor and the reasons other crops were rejected.
  • It shows expected income and field risks together, which helps farmers plan.
  • Crop rotation supports soil health.
  • It scores irrigated and rain-fed fields differently, which reflects Morocco’s water scarcity.

Intended impact

NextCrop aims to help smallholder farmers pick crops that fit their land and climate. That should mean fewer failed seasons, less wasted input, healthier soils and better use of scarce water. It also steers farmers away from crops that cannot tolerate saline soil. The wider goals are food security and adaptation to climate change in Morocco.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages and frameworks: The server is written in Python with Flask. The interface is a React web app built with Vite.
  • Mapping: Mapbox handles the field polygon.
  • Libraries: pandas and NumPy process the data and compute scores. rasterio reads the soil and salinity maps. Pillow handles satellite images, and requests calls the web services.
  • Data sources: NASA POWER supplies climate data and SoilGrids supplies soil data. Elevation comes from SRTM through OpenTopoData. The other sources are the FAO salinity raster, FAO ECOCROP for crop requirements, the FAO crop calendar for Morocco, FAOSTAT for yields and prices of 55 crops, and NASA GIBS MODIS Terra NDVI for vegetation.
  • Testing: An automated self-test simulates the climate service offline. It checks the data files, rotation logic, input validation and error handling.
  • Hardware: No special hardware is needed. A standard computer or cloud server runs one process that serves both the interface and the API.

What is creative about the project

  • One action, drawing a field on a map, pulls together climate, soil, altitude, salinity, satellite vegetation, crop calendar and price data.
  • It turns agronomic knowledge into a transparent scoring system and runs it on live open data.
  • It plans the rotation over time, so each sowing date follows the previous harvest.
  • It copes with messy real-world data. It merges synonymous crop names, estimates a sowing window for crops missing from the calendar, and skips missing values without stopping the analysis.
  • It converts colour-coded NASA satellite images into NDVI values, then into plain-language advice.
  • It explains why crops were rejected, which helps farmers trust the result.
  • The tool suggests a crop when it's time to actually plant it based on FAO crop calendar for Morocco dataset

Factors we considered

  • Local conditions: Morocco has six agricultural zones, each with its own sowing calendar.
  • Water: Irrigated and rain-fed fields are scored differently.
  • Altitude: The climate grid gives temperature for a cell, so the system corrects it to the field’s actual height.
  • Soil: The score uses pH, texture, depth, nitrogen and salinity.
  • Salinity: Crops are grouped by salt tolerance following FAO guidelines.
  • Rotation: Following the crop family order limits pests and soil exhaustion.
  • Data resolution: Pixels cover roughly 1 to 5 km, so scores are softened and no crop is banned outright on coarse data.
  • Reliability: When an external service is down, the system returns a clear error. When some data is missing, it tells the farmer.
  • Usability: The farmer only needs to draw a field, choose a month and name the last crop. Results are written in plain language.
  • Exclusion: The rotation does not cover trees or crops that take a long time to harvest, such as bananas and avocados. These plants stay in the same spot for years, so they cannot move through a five-stage cycle. NextCrop applies only to annual and seasonal crops.

Why NextCrop follows a five-stage rotation

NextCrop rotates crops in a fixed five-stage cycle: legumes, cereals (Poaceae), brassicas, umbellifers and alliums, then nightshades and cucurbits. The order is set by how each group changes the soil and which pests the next group meets.

Legumes come first. Bacteria in their roots fix nitrogen from the air, so the soil holds more nitrogen at harvest. Cereals come next and use that nitrogen. They belong to a different family from legumes, so they share few pests and diseases with them. Brassicas follow the cereals. They need a lot of nutrients and do well in soil that is free of legume diseases. Their residues release compounds that can suppress some soil pathogens and weeds. Umbellifers and alliums come fourth. They need less fertility than brassicas, so they suit soil that the previous crop has partly drained. Their different families and root depths break the brassicas’ pest cycles. Nightshades and cucurbits come last. They are heavy feeders and are prone to soil-borne diseases and nematodes, which build up when the same families return too soon. By the time they are planted, four other crop groups have grown in the field since the last nightshade or cucurbit. The cycle then returns to legumes, which restore the nitrogen these heavy feeders removed.

Each family returns only after four other groups have grown, which limits pest buildup and soil exhaustion. The order also alternates nitrogen-supplying, nitrogen-using and nutrient-demanding crops, so fertility stays balanced.
